text: Clark and Chalmers' 'parity principle,' the core of their extended-mind argument, states that:
choices: if a part of the world does a job that we would count as cognitive were it done in the head, then that part of the world is part of the cognitive process
mental states are identical to brain states of one specific physical type
the body, not just the brain, is the seat of all genuine cognition
two functionally identical systems must share all the same phenomenal states
explanation: The parity principle says location should not matter: functional role, not being inside the skull, is what makes a process cognitive -- so Otto's notebook can be part of his memory. Option 1 is the type-identity theory; option 2 is embodied cognition; option 3 is a functionalist thesis about qualia, not the parity principle.
